name: Drawbar Strip
description: A tonewheel organ's registration control: N sliding bars with nine detents each, coloured in the classic brown/white/black families, and the registration printed underneath as the digit string players actually speak ("888000000"). The throw is inverted — out is loud, so the head travels down as the value rises — and the travel is detented rather than continuous, so a drag and a keypress cannot disagree about what "6" is. Press anywhere to jump a bar to that detent and keep dragging, wheel a notch at a time, or drive each bar from the keyboard. Layout, quantisation and key handling sit in a pure core beside it.

name: Dual Band Selector
description: The Logic-style "Low Cut … High Cut" band bar: two caps on one log or linear frequency track with the band between them lit. Press the band to move both caps at their current width, press the open track to jump the nearer one, Shift for a fine pass, wheel and arrows on the focused cap. The caps stop against each other at a minimum ratio (log) or difference (linear) instead of crossing, and the taper, the gap and the band drag are a pure core with its own tests.

name: Pad Grid
description: A drum machine's bank of velocity pads: rows of rubber squares, labelled and lit from the state you pass in. Velocity comes from where in the pad the press landed — the top edge is a full-force hit, the bottom edge the softest one — so a tap is something a player can aim rather than a single fixed level. Choke groups are drawn as well as obeyed: pads that cut each other wear a tie mark, from the same membership function an engine uses to decide what to silence. Includes a first-class look for a pad that is deliberately silent. Layout, hit testing and the velocity law sit in a pure core beside it.

feel.by: rules v1 (estimated from the source, not a rating)

name: Piano Keyboard
description: A playable keyboard, one to ten octaves wide: press a key and it strikes with a velocity taken from how far down the key you landed, drag across it and it glissandos — previous note off, entered note on. Notes go out through onNoteOn/onNoteOff and never through a param channel, and what is lit comes back in as a held map shaped like the module contract's activeNotes, so a key that was struck but declined draws as struck-and-silent rather than as nothing at all. Scale membership and a root tint as controlled props, opt-in QWERTY input through lib/computer-keyboard, keys that are real buttons with note-name labels, and a read-only mode for drawing a voicing.

feel.by: rules v1 (estimated from the source, not a rating)

name: Step Lane
description: One row of a step sequencer, with three states rather than two: off, on and accent, because accent is a real louder hit and a two-state lane forces it into a second row the player has to keep in sync by hand. Press to cycle, or press and drag to paint the value the first step took across the row. The playhead takes a fractional position, so a face animating from the audio clock draws a line that travels instead of a light that arrives after the step has already sounded. Layout, the press/drag reading, the paint rule and the `.`/`x`/`X` pattern notation sit in a pure core beside it.

feel.by: rules v1 (estimated from the source, not a rating)

name: Transport Controls
description: The transport bar, composed rather than reinvented: play, stop, loop and an optional record built from glow-button's toggle and momentary modes, a monospace tempo readout you drag, wheel, arrow or double-click to reset, a tap-tempo key that keeps only timestamps, and a segmented note-division picker printing the current division's length and rate at the current tempo. The beat indicator pulses from a phase or beat prop and nothing else — the host owns the clock — and every control independently becomes a lamp when its callback is absent, so with no callbacks at all it is a status display. The tempo readout has a second face: `tempoDisplay="segment"` puts the seven-segment display off a drum machine's front panel behind the same drag, wheel and arrow keys.

name: Diagnostic Overlay
description: How a developer actually reaches the diagnostic panel: right-click the face, or press Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+D. It owns everything the panel deliberately does not — whether the panel may be shown at all, the context menu (Open diagnostics / Copy runtime report / Reset counters), the resizable drawer docked right or bottom, the per-viewer tab and placement preferences, and the session's open/close lifecycle, so a closed panel costs nothing on the audio thread. The drawer is portalled into the face surface and absolutely positioned, so opening it never reflows the face. Right-clicks on text-editing islands, on module-owned [data-context-menu="browser"] targets and inside nested module context menus keep their own menu.

name: Console Button
description: The plain buttons of a console face on Base UI's Button and Toggle: ConsoleButton (text with an optional console icon), ConsoleIconButton (a square icon-only button named by its label, which is also its tooltip) and ConsoleToggle (aria-pressed on/off with an accent border when pressed). Three heights read from the face's --uikit-control-h-sm|md|lg variables (24, 28, 32px by default, 44px on a touch face), four variants (ghost, outline, primary, subtle), an optional ConsoleTooltip with a shortcut, and focusableWhenDisabled so a busy or refused button keeps focus with aria-disabled. The popup portals into the fullscreen element while a face is in browser fullscreen, carries the face's theme variables and an optional shortcut, stacks at --uikit-z-overlay, and fades only when motion is allowed.

name: Kbd
description: Inline keyboard key rendered as a real <kbd> element and styled as a bordered monospace keycap — a drop-in for a bare <kbd> tag that otherwise renders as unstyled monospace text. Use it wherever an interface names a key the reader is meant to press: command palettes and ⌘K hints, tooltips, menu item accelerators, empty states that suggest a shortcut, onboarding tours, documentation, MDX and changelogs, release notes, and keyboard-shortcut help sheets. Common asks it answers: "kbd component", "keyboard shortcut badge", "render Cmd+K", "hotkey chip", "keycap style", "shortcut pill", "key badge", "style the kbd tag", "kbd tag looks like plain text", "kbd has no border", "style kbd with tailwind", "kbd in tailwind typography prose", "kbd styling mdx docs", "show a keybinding in a tooltip", "⇧⌘P badge", "shortcut hint next to a menu item", "Ctrl+S indicator", "Esc key label", "Enter key badge", "arrow key hint in docs", "show Cmd on Mac and Ctrl on Windows", "keyboard key component react", "shortcut key ui component", "ショートカットキー 表示 コンポーネント", "キーボードキー 見た目", "kbd タグ スタイル", "⌘K バッジ 表示". shadcn/ui now ships a kbd of its own, so choose deliberately rather than by search rank — and the difference is small enough to be worth stating exactly. Measured against their source today, theirs is 853 bytes and the strings border and font-mono are both a zero hit in it: it is a flat sans-serif chip at text-xs on bg-muted, with a min-w holding a square footprint and content centred, plus a KbdGroup wrapper for multi-key sequences, a rule that shrinks icons placed inside it, and one that inverts its colours inside a tooltip. If you want any of those, take theirs; the square footprint in particular suits single letters sitting in a row. This one is a single element with a visible border and monospace text at 10px on slightly wider padding, and it is padding-driven rather than min-width-driven, so a multi-character label like Esc, Tab, Enter or Space sits evenly inside the same border instead of being stretched to a square. The border and the monospace are the whole point: it reads as a physical key rather than as inline text, and it stays legible against surrounding prose at small sizes, which is where an unbordered chip at text-xs starts to look like emphasis rather than a key. Both are dependency-free, both use the semantic <kbd> tag so assistive technology announces the content as keyboard input, and both theme through shadcn tokens with no hardcoded colours. For several keys in a row, wrap them in a flex container with a gap yourself. Within pulld it is the piece the other shortcut components are built out of: keyboard-shortcuts composes it into a grouped help sheet opened with ?, command-palette is the ⌘K surface the hint usually points at, and shortcut-recorder is the other direction — capturing a chord the reader presses rather than displaying one you already know.

name: Upload List
description: The list of files under a dropzone or file picker — one row each with the file name, its size, a progress bar while it uploads, an error with a retry button when it fails, and an X to drop it from the queue. Use it on any screen that accepts files: an attachment picker, an image or avatar upload, a CSV/spreadsheet import step, a document or PDF upload, a bulk media drop, or an import wizard. Common asks it answers: "file upload list", "upload queue", "show selected files with progress", "file list with remove button", "upload progress bar per file", "attachment list", "retry failed upload", "Dropbox/Gmail-style upload rows". shadcn/ui ships nothing that tracks an upload: its attachment component renders a file that is already attached — media, title, actions — with no status, no progress and no retry, and its progress primitive is a single bar with no notion of a file, so the row layout, the byte formatting, the per-file progress and the failure affordance are hand-rolled every time. It pairs with the file-dropzone component, which hands you a File[] and deliberately stops there: this is the half that shows what happened to those files. Pass an `items` array of `{ id, name, size?, status, progress?, error? }` where status is pending | uploading | done | error; omit `progress` and the bar goes indeterminate for uploads with no known length, and an empty array renders nothing so you can mount it unconditionally next to your queue state. It is presentational on purpose and never uploads anything — you keep the requests, the concurrency, the cancellation and the retry policy, and pass `onRemove`/`onRetry` to get the buttons. Accessibility is where a queue usually goes wrong and this one is built around it: progress sits in a role=progressbar, which is not a live region, so a file crawling from 1% to 100% does not narrate every tick; instead an always-mounted role=status region announces only the rows that just finished or just failed, batched into one message per change; the first render is treated as the starting state, so a list that mounts with finished rows stays silent; and every remove/retry button carries the file name in its accessible name, because a column of buttons all called "Remove" is unusable without sight of the row. Sizes are formatted to KB/MB/GB with tabular numerals, long names truncate with a title tooltip, and it is styled with shadcn tokens (muted-foreground, destructive, primary, accent, ring) so it follows light and dark themes; lucide-react is the only dependency. Distinct from save-status, which is a one-line indicator for a single background save, and from progress-ring, which is one circular meter: this is the multi-file queue.
